title: The Letter Lincoln Never Sent
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie
wiifm: This is the book behind every customer service script and every management course you have ever sat through. You work with people who are frightened, ashamed or angry about money, and you manage people too, so how you criticise, listen and ask matters every day. Today you follow Dale Carnegie, a poor Missouri farm boy who failed as an actor, sold lard, and turned a refused job into the best-selling book on dealing with people ever written. You will also face the hardest question about it: does any of this work if you do not mean it?

b: Dale Carnagey, as his name was then spelled, was born in November 1888 on a farm near Maryville, Missouri. His family was poor. The farm flooded, the crops failed, and his mother was a devout Methodist who hoped he would become a preacher or a teacher.

He went to the state teachers college at Warrensburg, and because the family could not afford lodgings in town, he rode to classes on horseback from the farm. He was poor, awkward and keenly aware of it. What changed him was public speaking. He threw himself into the college debating contests, lost again and again, and kept going until he started to win.

It is worth noticing where his method came from. Carnegie was not a born charmer. He was an anxious young man who learned, by repeated failure in front of audiences, that people respond to someone who seems genuinely interested in them. Everything in his book was learned the hard way first.
ch.cap: Dale rides to college across flooded Missouri farmland

ch.h: Bacon, soap and a failed stage career
b: After college he sold correspondence courses to ranchers, then took a job selling bacon, soap and lard for Armour and Company out of the stockyards of South Omaha. He was successful, and he quit anyway, because he wanted something more.
He went to New York and studied at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, then toured as an actor in a road production of a play called Polly of the Circus. He decided he had no future on the stage.

So by his early twenties he had tried teaching, selling and acting, and failed to settle at any of them. Look at what he had gathered, though: a debater's nerve, a salesman's ear for what customers want, and an actor's sense of how an audience feels. It was the perfect kit for what came next.
ch.cap: Selling bacon and soap at the stockyards of Omaha

b: In 1912 the failed actor walked into the YMCA on 125th Street in New York and asked to be paid two dollars an evening to teach a class in public speaking. The YMCA said no.

Instead of arguing, he restructured the deal. Pay me nothing, he offered, and give me a share of the profits from the class instead. They agreed, because it cost them nothing. According to the introduction to his own book, within three years they were paying him thirty dollars a night on that basis.

It is a lovely first scene for the man who would write the century's great book on handling people. His very first recorded move, faced with a refusal, was not to push harder but to find a version of the deal the other side could say yes to. In the years that followed he built his course across the country. In the early nineteen-twenties he changed the spelling of his name to Carnegie, which happened to echo the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who was no relation.
ch.cap: Refused two dollars, he takes a share instead

ch.h: The course that became a book
b: The book was not his idea. In 1934 Leon Shimkin, an executive at the publisher Simon and Schuster, took Carnegie's fourteen-week course, was impressed, and spent months trying to persuade him to write it up. Carnegie resisted. In the end Shimkin hired a stenographer to take down the lectures and gave Carnegie the transcript to edit.
That is why the book reads as it does: in the second person, with a story every minute or so, and the principles repeated at the end of each chapter like a teacher making sure the back row has heard.

It came out in 1936 and sold a quarter of a million copies in three months. It sold millions in Carnegie's lifetime and many millions since, and it still sells steadily. One detail almost every account gets wrong: the original had six parts, including one on writing letters and one on a happier home life. The familiar four-part version is the 1981 revision, which dropped those two.

His classes were not lectures in the usual sense. Students, mostly salesmen, clerks and managers, stood up and told short stories from their own lives about dealing with people, and Carnegie collected the ones that worked. That is why the book is full of names of ordinary people and their small victories. It is a record of experiments carried out by thousands of students in offices and shops across America.
ch.cap: A stenographer types the course into a book

ch.h: Even gangsters think they are good
b: Carnegie opens not with advice but with criminals. He points to Al Capone, the gangster Dutch Schultz and a young killer called Francis Two Gun Crowley, and observes that none of them saw himself as a bad man. Crowley, besieged by police in a New York apartment in 1931, wrote a note saying that under his coat was a weary heart, but a kind one.

The argument is simple. If men like these can build a self-justification strong enough to survive a gunfight, the ordinary person you are about to criticise will have no trouble at all. Criticism does not correct people. It makes them defend themselves, resent you and hunt for excuses, and it does so automatically. Hence his first principle: do not criticise, condemn or complain.

There is an irony worth noticing. Carnegie's own figures in this opening are off. He says a hundred and fifty police surrounded Crowley; contemporary accounts suggest around three hundred, firing hundreds of rounds into the building over about two hours. Crowley was nineteen and was executed at Sing Sing in January 1932. And the weary heart letter is known only through Carnegie. The book's opening story, about people who polish their own version of events, is itself a little polished.
ch.cap: Besieged, Two Gun Crowley writes that his heart is kind

b: Carnegie's best illustration of restraint is documented to the letter. In July 1863, days after the Battle of Gettysburg, Abraham Lincoln watched his general, George Meade, fail to attack Robert E. Lee's beaten army as it waited to cross the flooded Potomac. The river fell, and Lee escaped. The war went on for almost two more years.
Lincoln sat down and wrote to Meade exactly what he thought: that Meade did not appreciate the magnitude of the misfortune in Lee's escape, and that his golden opportunity was gone.
He never sent it. The letter was found among his papers after his assassination, with a note in his secretary's hand saying it had never been sent or signed. It is in the Library of Congress today.

What is extraordinary is that Lincoln wrote the whole thing first. He did not swallow his anger. He put it down in full, and writing it was what made sending it unnecessary. That is Carnegie's principle in a single object: say it to the page, not to the person.

Carnegie draws a second lesson from Lincoln's life. As a young man in Illinois, Lincoln had written mocking letters about his rivals and published them in the local newspaper. One of them so enraged a politician named James Shields that he challenged Lincoln to a duel in 1842. The two men met on a sandbar in the Mississippi before friends stopped the fight. Lincoln, Carnegie says, never again wrote an insulting letter or ridiculed anyone in public. The restraint of 1863 had been learned twenty years earlier, the hard way.
ch.cap: Lincoln writes his fury to Meade, then files it away

b: Carnegie's third principle is the one people skip: arouse in the other person an eager want. His illustration is his own. He was very fond of strawberries and cream, but fish, for some strange reason, prefer worms. So when he went fishing, he thought about what the fish wanted, not what he wanted.

It sounds obvious until you notice how often it is ignored. Almost every request in business describes the requester's need. We need this signed by Friday. I'm chasing invoice number so-and-so. Each is strawberries and cream offered to a fish. The fix takes a minute: rewrite each sentence so the subject is the other person and the verb is something they gain or avoid.

Try it on your three most-used messages: the follow-up, the covering note on a quote and the chase for a missing document. Count the sentences that start with we or I. Then rewrite them so the subject is you and the verb is something the reader gains or stops losing. The request does not change. The way into the other person's attention does.

Part Two of the book is the famous part. Become genuinely interested in other people. Smile. Remember that a person's name is to them the sweetest sound in any language. Be a good listener. Talk in terms of their interests. Make them feel important, and do it sincerely.

The evidence is more mixed than fans or cynics admit. People do prefer the letters in their own name, and we notice our own name even in a conversation we are not following, so names really do grab attention. The bolder claim that name preference shapes life choices, like where we live or what job we take, is still disputed. And the idea that forcing a smile makes you happier has had mixed results in large replication studies, failing in one and showing a small effect in another.
ch.cap: He likes strawberries and cream; the fish want worms

b: Part Three opens with the line that makes the book either wise or infuriating: the only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it. Then come the rules. Never tell someone they are wrong. If you are wrong, admit it quickly. Let the other person do most of the talking. Let them feel the idea is theirs. Try honestly to see things from their point of view.

Read that beside Tuesday's book and the overlap is uncanny. Letting the other person talk is Voss's mirror. Seeing their point of view is tactical empathy. Admitting fault quickly is the accusation audit. Eighty years apart, a Missouri farm boy and an FBI negotiator arrived at the same tools. But note the difference: Carnegie has no account of power. When interests truly clash, his advice to avoid the argument usually means the weaker side gives way and calls it tact.

Part Four is written from the manager's chair. Begin with praise. Point out mistakes indirectly. Talk about your own mistakes first. Ask questions instead of giving orders. Let people save face. Give them a fine reputation to live up to. His example is Charles Schwab, who was paid over a million dollars a year by the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie and said his greatest asset was his ability to arouse enthusiasm among his people through appreciation and encouragement. Carnegie's version is a little generous. Schwab knew a great deal about making steel, and the million included bonuses.

Two of these management principles are worth more than the rest, and both are about order rather than sentiment. Talking about your own mistakes before correcting someone shows the standard applies to you too, so it survives after you leave the room. And asking how would you get this done by Thursday produces a plan the other person owns, where saying get this done by Thursday produces compliance you must police yourself.
ch.cap: Schwab praises his men beside the blazing furnace

b: Now the passage that should stay with you. To illustrate beginning in a friendly way, Carnegie describes John D. Rockefeller Junior in 1915, addressing representatives of the miners of the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. Rockefeller opened by calling it a red-letter day in his life. Carnegie reports admiringly that the men went back to work without another word about the wages they had been fighting for.

What he leaves out is what happened the year before. On 20 April 1914, at Ludlow, Colorado, the state National Guard and company guards attacked a tent colony of striking miners' families. Around twenty-one people died, including eleven children. Rockefeller controlled the company and had backed its hard line. His charm offensive was shaped with Ivy Lee, often called the founder of modern public relations. And the strike had in fact already collapsed in December 1914, months before the speech, so Carnegie's tidy ending is doubtful too.

So the book's model of friendliness is a staged reputational exercise by the owner of a company whose guards had helped kill children, and Carnegie presents it as a success. This is a deeper problem than insincerity. The techniques do not care what they are used for. They work for Rockefeller as well as for you, and the book gives you no way of telling the two apart.
ch.cap: Rockefeller's charm, months after the Ludlow tents burned

b: The novelist Sinclair Lewis mocked the book as a manual for pretending interest in people in order to get things out of them. Carnegie saw the charge coming and answered with the word he uses more than any other: sincerely. Honest, sincere appreciation, he says, is the difference between praise and flattery.
The trouble is that a technique for sincerity sounds like a contradiction, and his own Rockefeller example proves the techniques work whether you mean them or not.

Here is a better way to read him. Nearly every one of his principles is, read kindly, an instruction to do a real thing rather than perform it. Become genuinely interested in other people is not a manner. It is a habit of attention, built by asking better questions. See things from their point of view is not a phrase. It is ten minutes of honest thought before a meeting. The techniques are hollow when performed and powerful when the underlying act is actually carried out, and they have lasted because most people, most of the time, never carry it out.

Carnegie spent his later years applying his method to the inside of the head as well. In 1948 he published How to Stop Worrying and Start Living, built in the same way from his students' stories, and the courses carrying his name kept spreading around the world after his death. The rules were simple enough to teach to anyone. The difficulty, then as now, was never learning them. It was meaning them.

Dale Carnegie died in New York in November 1955, by then one of the most famous teachers in the world. His life began with a poor boy riding to college and losing debates, and his lasting lesson is the one he learned there. You cannot move people you have not bothered to understand, and no technique can stand in for the bother.
ch.cap: Old Carnegie leans in and truly listens

take: Write it, then do not send it
Lincoln wrote his furious letter in full and kept it in a drawer. Draft the angry email to a lender or colleague, then sleep on it before sending anything.
Even killers justify themselves. When something goes wrong with staff or a partner, start with what went right and ask questions instead of condemning.
Bait the hook for the fish
Rewrite chase emails, quote notes and follow-ups so each sentence is about what the reader gains or avoids, not what you need.
Carnegie answered the YMCA's no by offering a profit share. When someone turns down your terms, look for a version of the deal they can say yes to.
Names genuinely grab attention. Use a client's name naturally, but do not expect it to work magic if the rest of the conversation ignores them.
Mentioning your own error before correcting someone shows the standard applies to you too, and makes the correction stick.
Give a reputation to live up to
Praise one specific strength, once, in front of others. Said precisely it tends to become true; said often and vaguely it becomes noise.
Rockefeller's friendliness worked after Ludlow. Influence skills serve any purpose, so check what you are using them for, especially with vulnerable clients.

The speech was shaped with the PR pioneer Ivy Lee. It shows the techniques work regardless of purpose, and the book gives no way to tell good uses from bad.
note: Documented: Carnegie's Missouri childhood, Armour sales job, acting school and Polly of the Circus tour, the 1912 YMCA arrangement as told in his own introduction, Shimkin's role, the 1936 publication and the 1981 revision, and his death in 1955. Lincoln's unsent letter of 14 July 1863 is in the Library of Congress. The Crowley siege of 1931 is documented, but Carnegie's police numbers are low and the weary heart letter is known only through him. The source said Rockefeller's speech came fourteen months after Ludlow; it was in 1915, more than a year later, and the strike had formally ended in December 1914, so Carnegie's ending is doubtful. Research on name preference and facial feedback remains contested.
words: To try to win someone's favour, often by flattery or calculated friendliness.
Sinclair Lewis mocked Carnegie's book as a manual for ingratiating yourself with people in order to get things out of them.
A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage.
Carnegie drew his line between praise and flattery with the word sincerely, insisting his method was the opposite of the sycophant's.
Generosity of spirit, especially towards a rival or someone who has let you down.
Lincoln's unsent letter to Meade is magnanimity in a single object: the anger written in full, then kept in a drawer.
A wealthy and powerful figure in a particular industry.
Carnegie changed the spelling of his name in the nineteen-twenties, echoing the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who was no relation.
Intended to calm anger and win goodwill.
Rockefeller's conciliatory speech to the Colorado miners was shaped with the publicist Ivy Lee, a year after the deaths at Ludlow.
stories: Two dollars a night, or nothing

To show the power of a friendly opening, Carnegie tells how John D. Rockefeller Junior addressed miners of the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company in 1915, called it a red-letter day in his life, and charmed them back to work. What Carnegie leaves out is the year before. On 20 April 1914, at Ludlow, Colorado, the National Guard and company guards attacked a tent colony of striking miners' families, and around twenty-one people died, eleven of them children. biz: Carnegie loved strawberries and cream, but he baited his hook with worms, because that is what fish want. Most chase messages describe the sender's need: we need your payslips, I am following up on your enquiry. This week, take your three most-used HomeownersLoan WhatsApp templates, the follow-up, the document chase and the note that goes with a quote, and count the sentences that start with we or I. Rewrite them so the subject is the customer and the verb is something they truthfully gain, such as: once your payslips are in, the lender can look at your application properly. Measure reply rate and documents returned within forty-eight hours.
Mean it, or don't do it

The Ludlow story is the book's warning: the techniques work whether you mean them or not. At Debt Support Direct, warmth with a client in distress must never become leverage. Make sincerity something you can check. In each call note, record the one thing the client said matters most, such as keeping the house or stopping the calls, and in weekly call reviews ask whether the recommendation actually served it. Use Lincoln's habit for complaints too: write the angry reply, leave it in the drawer, then send the calm one. Measure complaint outcomes and how often recommendations match clients' stated goals.
connects: Carnegie's Rockefeller example proves what Machiavelli argued openly, that techniques of seeming work whatever the intentions of the person using them.
Carnegie's rule never to criticise, because everyone believes they are in the right, echoes Marcus Aurelius reminding himself each morning that people do wrong from their own sense of what is good.
Voss's tactical empathy rediscovers Carnegie's rules of listening and seeing the other side's view, but adds the account of power and conflict that Carnegie lacks.
recap:
Dale Carnagey, as his name was first spelled, was born on a poor Missouri farm in eighteen eighty-eight. He rode to college on horseback because his family could not afford lodgings in town, and he was awkward and knew it. What changed him was debating. He lost again and again, kept going, and learned that people respond to someone who seems genuinely interested in them.

He sold bacon and soap for Armour and Company, quit, trained as an actor, and decided he had no future on the stage. Then in nineteen twelve he asked a YMCA in Harlem for two dollars a night to teach public speaking. They refused, so he offered to work for a share of the profits instead, and within three years he was earning thirty dollars a night. His first recorded move, faced with a no, was to find a version of the deal the other side could say yes to.

His course spread across America, and in nineteen thirty-six a publisher who had taken it persuaded him to turn it into a book. It sold a quarter of a million copies in three months and has sold many millions since.

The ideas are simple. Do not criticise, condemn or complain, because even gangsters believe they are good, and criticism only makes people defend themselves. Lincoln showed the way when he wrote a furious letter to the general who let Lee escape, and never sent it. Arouse in the other person an eager want, because fish prefer worms, however much you like strawberries and cream. Be genuinely interested in people, use their names, listen, and let them do most of the talking. Avoid arguments, admit your mistakes quickly, ask questions instead of giving orders, and let people save face.

But the book has a dark page. Carnegie praises John D. Rockefeller Junior for winning over miners with a friendly speech, and never mentions that a year earlier, at Ludlow in Colorado, guards and troops had attacked the miners' tent colony and children had died. The techniques do not care who uses them. And Carnegie has no account of power, so avoiding an argument often means the weaker side gives way.

His answer to the cynics was one word, sincerely. Read kindly, nearly every rule is an instruction to do a real thing rather than perform it. The rules are easy to learn. The hard part is meaning them.

The line to remember is the lesson of the farm boy who lost all those debates. You cannot move people you have not bothered to understand.
